pll2d8c1-d1e3514.summary: Notes the question among the learned whether all angels, good and bad, are corporeal, having bodies united to them.

pll2d8c1-d1e3517.summary: Reports some who, relying on Augustine, think all angels had aerial bodies from the purer air, fit for acting not suffering; the good kept these, so fine they cannot be seen unless clothed in a grosser form; the bad angels' bodies were changed at their fall into thicker air, able to suffer from fire.
claims: Some hold angels have aerial bodies.

pll2d8c1-d1e3523.summary: Cites Augustine on Genesis: demons are called aerial animals because of their aerial bodies, not dissolved by death, since air is more apt to act than suffer; the fallen angels with their prince were thrust into the dark air and perhaps changed into an aerial quality able to suffer from fire, the air being their prison until judgment.

pll2d8c1-d1e3544.summary: Notes that Augustine seems to teach what some think about angelic bodies.

pll2d8c1-d1e3550.summary: Reports others who say Augustine was reporting others' opinion, since he says 'are called,' not 'are,' though he asserted their dwelling in the dark air. Many Catholic writers agree that angels are incorporeal and have no bodies united to them, but assume bodies prepared by God for their ministry and lay them down afterward; in these they appeared and spoke, sometimes in God's person without distinction, sometimes as Father, Son, or Holy Spirit.
claims: Angels have spoken in God's person.

pl-l2d8c1.summary: Asks whether angels, good and bad, are corporeal, having bodies united to them. Some, following Augustine, think all angels had aerial bodies of the purer upper air before fall or confirmation, fit for acting not suffering, invisible unless clothed in a grosser form; the good kept them, while the bad angels' bodies were changed at the fall into thicker air, able to suffer from fire. Augustine on Genesis says demons are called aerial animals. Others say Augustine was reporting others' opinion ('are called,' not 'are'), but asserted their dwelling in the dark air; many Catholic writers teach that angels are incorporeal, assuming bodies when God prepares them for their ministry and laying them aside afterward, appearing and speaking in them, sometimes in the person of God or of a divine person.
claims: Some hold angels have aerial bodies, the good keeping fine ones and the bad changed to grosser ones.
Augustine calls demons 'aerial animals,' perhaps reporting others' opinion.
Many Catholic writers teach that angels are incorporeal.
Angels assume bodies for their ministry and lay them aside afterward.
In assumed bodies angels appeared and spoke, sometimes in God's person.
